lead: Chemical reaction equilibria tells you how far a reaction can go, not how fast. After this unit you can write stoichiometric tables with extent, apply the Gibbs minimum criterion, evaluate K at any temperature, and solve single or multiple reactions for equilibrium composition, conversion and yield.
about: This unit turns stoichiometry and Gibbs energy into quantitative equilibrium predictions. 7.1 sets mole balances with extent ξ. 7.2 states the minimum-G criterion and Σνᵢμᵢ = 0. 7.3 defines standard Gibbs energy change and the activity-based equilibrium constant. 7.4 gives van't Hoff temperature dependence. 7.5 evaluates K and converts it to composition. 7.6 separates feasibility (Q versus K) from equilibrium conversion and yield. 7.7 shows how pressure and inerts move gas-phase equilibria without changing K. 7.8 extends the method to gas nonideality, pure solids, and several simultaneous reactions.

chapters.idea: Every reacting mixture can be described by stoichiometric coefficients and one extent variable per independent reaction.
chapters.depth: Stoichiometric coefficients νᵢ with sign convention: negative for reactants, positive for products. Mole balance nᵢ = nᵢ₀ + νᵢξ for one reaction; total moles nT = nT₀ + ξΣνᵢ. For r independent reactions use ξ₁...ξr and nᵢ = nᵢ₀ + Σⱼ νᵢⱼξⱼ. Define limiting reactant and conversion X = (nᵢ₀ − nᵢ)/nᵢ₀. Include inerts. Some syllabi call ξ the reaction coordinate.

figure.title: Mole table for ammonia synthesis
figure.aria: A species-by-species table showing initial moles, stoichiometric coefficients and final moles at extent 4 mol.

chapters.example: Feed 10 mol N2 and 30 mol H2 to the reaction N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3. At extent ξ = 4 mol, find n_N2, n_H2, n_NH3 and total moles. ν_N2 = −1, ν_H2 = −3, ν_NH3 = +2. n_N2 = 10 − 4 = 6 mol; n_H2 = 30 − 12 = 18 mol; n_NH3 = 0 + 8 = 8 mol; total = 32 mol.
chapters.trap: Using one extent for two independent reactions, or taking conversion as ξ divided by total moles. Divide by initial moles of the limiting reactant; ν carries the sign.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 mole balances; Unit 2 heat of reaction for later energy work.
chapters.leave: Equilibrium criterion to 7.2; conversion and yield definitions to 7.6.

chapters.idea: At fixed temperature and pressure a closed reacting system reaches equilibrium when total Gibbs energy is minimum, equivalently Σνᵢμᵢ = 0.
chapters.depth: G = Σnᵢμᵢ; dG = Σμᵢ dnᵢ = (Σνᵢμᵢ)dξ at fixed T and P. Equilibrium when dG/dξ = 0, so Σνᵢμᵢ = 0; second derivative positive for stable minimum. Define reaction Gibbs energy ΔGr = Σνᵢμᵢ and affinity A = −ΔGr. For heterogeneous reactions each species has equal μ in every phase where it appears, plus one reaction equation per independent reaction. Reacting phase rule F = N − P + 2 − r for N species, P phases, r independent reactions. Duhem's theorem: fixing two intensive variables fixes the intensive state for specified initial amounts. Some syllabi call Σνᵢμᵢ = 0 the chemical equilibrium criterion.

figure.aria: A U-shaped curve of total Gibbs energy against extent; the minimum at ξ = 2 mol is equilibrium.

chapters.example: For a single reaction at 500 K and 1 bar, the reaction Gibbs energy at a trial composition is ΔGr = −8.0 kJ/mol. Find the direction of reaction. ΔGr = Σνᵢμᵢ; negative means dG/dξ < 0, so G falls as ξ increases. The reaction proceeds forward. At equilibrium ΔGr = 0.
chapters.trap: Setting ΔG° = 0 at equilibrium. Equilibrium requires ΔGr = Σνᵢμᵢ = 0; ΔG° is a fixed standard-state quantity.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 Gibbs energy; Unit 5 chemical potential.
chapters.leave: Equilibrium constant to 7.3; phase equilibrium details to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The standard Gibbs energy change fixes the equilibrium constant through activities relative to standard states.
chapters.depth: ΔG° = Σνᵢμᵢ° = ΣνᵢΔGf° for formation data. K = Π aᵢ^νᵢ = exp(−ΔG°/RT). Activities: gas aᵢ = fᵢ/fᵢ° ≈ φᵢ yᵢ P/P°; ideal gas aᵢ = yᵢ P/P°; liquid aᵢ = γᵢ xᵢ with pure liquid standard state. Choice of standard state changes μᵢ° and K together. For ideal gas, K = Ky (P/P°)^Σν, where Ky = Π yᵢ^νᵢ; K = Kc (RT/P°)^Σν if Kc uses concentrations. Reversing a reaction inverts K; doubling it squares K.

figure.title: From standard states to K
figure.aria: A flow from standard chemical potentials to standard Gibbs energy change to K and finally to the activity product.

chapters.example: For A ⇌ 2B at 400 K, ΔG° = +5.0 kJ/mol. R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Find K. ΔG° = 5000 J/mol. ln K = −ΔG°/(RT) = −5000/(8.314×400) = −1.503. K = e^−1.503 = 0.222. K is dimensionless.
chapters.trap: Writing K as partial pressures in bar and calling it dimensionless. Use activities; for gases divide pᵢ by P° (usually 1 bar).
chapters.prereq: 7.1 stoichiometry; 7.2 equilibrium criterion; Unit 5 fugacity and activity.
chapters.leave: Temperature dependence to 7.4; composition calculation to 7.5.

chapters.idea: The equilibrium constant changes with temperature according to the standard enthalpy of reaction.
chapters.depth: van't Hoff: d ln K/dT = ΔH°/(RT²). For constant ΔH°, ln(K₂/K₁) = −(ΔH°/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁). Endothermic ΔH° > 0 gives K rising with T; exothermic gives K falling. If ΔCp is significant, use ΔH°(T) = ΔH°(T₀) + ∫ΔCp dT and ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°; integrate numerically. Le Chatelier gives the same sign rule.

figure.aria: A straight line of ln K against 1/T for an exothermic reaction; slope is −ΔH°/R.

chapters.trap: Using T in °C or reversing the sign. Use kelvin and keep ΔH° sign; exothermic K falls when T rises.
chapters.prereq: 7.3 equilibrium constant; Unit 2 heat of reaction.

chapters.idea: K is evaluated from thermodynamic data and then converted into mixture composition through activities and mole balances.
chapters.depth: Evaluate ΔG° from standard Gibbs energies of formation at 298 K, or from ΔH° − TΔS°, then correct to operating T with van't Hoff. Build K expression in activities. For ideal gas, substitute yᵢ = nᵢ/nT and nᵢ = nᵢ₀ + νᵢξ; solve one algebraic equation in ξ. For liquid, use γᵢ xᵢ. Check by back-substitution. Some syllabi call this relation of K to composition.

figure.aria: The reaction quotient curve crosses the horizontal K line at ξ = 0.229 mol.

chapters.example: At 400 K, A ⇌ 2B has K = 0.222. Feed 1 mol pure A at P = 1 bar; P° = 1 bar. Find equilibrium ξ and mole fractions. n_A = 1−ξ, n_B = 2ξ, nT = 1+ξ. For ideal gas, K = (P/P°)^1 y_B²/y_A = 4ξ²/(1−ξ²). Solve 0.222 = 4ξ²/(1−ξ²): ξ² = 0.222/4.222 = 0.05258, ξ = 0.229 mol. y_A = (1−0.229)/1.229 = 0.627; y_B = 2(0.229)/1.229 = 0.373.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that total moles change with ξ, or using yᵢ directly in K when Σν ≠ 0 and P ≠ P°.
chapters.prereq: 7.1 mole balances; 7.3 K expression; 7.4 temperature correction.

chapters.idea: Feasibility is judged by Q versus K at the current composition, while equilibrium conversion and yield measure how far the feed can go.
chapters.depth: Reaction quotient Q = Π aᵢ^νᵢ at current composition. ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q = RT ln(Q/K). Q < K forward, Q > K backward, Q = K equilibrium. Feasibility at given T and P uses ΔG sign; K > 1 only says standard-state favorability. For single reaction, equilibrium conversion X = (nᵢ₀ − nᵢ)/nᵢ₀ for limiting reactant. Yield: moles of desired product formed divided by moles of limiting reactant fed, on a stoichiometric basis; selectivity compares desired to undesired product. Solve K with mole balances.

figure.title: Q compared with K
figure.aria: A decision flow: compute Q, compare with K, choose forward, equilibrium or backward, and read equilibrium conversion.

chapters.example: For A ⇌ 2B, K = 0.222 at 400 K, feed 1 mol A at 1 bar. At ξ = 0.10 mol, Q = 4ξ²/(1−ξ²) = 0.0404. At ξ = 0.30 mol, Q = 0.396. State direction at each ξ. Q(0.10) = 0.0404 < K, so forward. Q(0.30) = 0.396 > K, so backward. At equilibrium ξ = 0.229 mol, conversion of A = 0.229/1 = 0.229 or 22.9%; yield of B = 2ξ/1 = 0.459 mol B per mol A fed.
chapters.trap: Reporting K > 1 as high conversion. Conversion also depends on stoichiometry, pressure and feed; yield is not selectivity.
chapters.leave: Pressure and inert effects to 7.7; multiple reactions to 7.8.

chapters.idea: Pressure and inert dilution shift gas-phase equilibrium composition without changing K at fixed temperature.
chapters.depth: For ideal gas K = Ky (P/P°)^Σν. Ky = K (P/P°)^−Σν. At fixed T, K is fixed; changing P changes Ky and composition. If Σν < 0, higher P favours products; if Σν > 0, lower P favours products; if Σν = 0, pressure has no ideal-gas effect. Inerts add total moles and dilute reactants, acting like lower partial pressures; they shift toward the side with more moles. Volume change at fixed T mirrors pressure. For liquids pressure effect is small except near critical or high P.

figure.aria: Equilibrium conversion of A falls as pressure rises for a reaction that makes more moles.

chapters.example: For A ⇌ 2B, K = 0.222 at 400 K. Feed 1 mol A. At P = 1 bar, ξ = 0.229 (X = 22.9%). Find X at P = 0.5 bar and P = 2 bar. K = (P/P°) 4ξ²/(1−ξ²). At P = 0.5 bar: 0.222 = 0.5×4ξ²/(1−ξ²), so ξ = 0.316, X = 31.6%. At P = 2 bar: 0.222 = 2×4ξ²/(1−ξ²), so ξ = 0.164, X = 16.4%. With 1 mol inert at 1 bar: K = 4ξ²/[(2+ξ)(1−ξ)], giving ξ = 0.299, X = 29.9%.
chapters.trap: Saying pressure changes K. At fixed T, K is constant; pressure changes activities and Ky.

chapters.idea: Real systems combine gas nonideality, multiple phases and several independent reactions, each with its own equilibrium relation and shared mole balances.
chapters.depth: Gas-phase: K = Π(φᵢ yᵢ P/P°)^νᵢ; use an equation of state for φᵢ. Heterogeneous: pure solids and pure liquids have activity 1 when their standard state is the pure phase at T and P; only gases or solutes enter K. Liquid-phase: K = Π(γᵢ xᵢ)^νᵢ. Simultaneous reactions: r independent reactions need r equilibrium constants and r extents ξⱼ; solve with shared mole balances and element balances. Apply reacting phase rule F = N − P + 2 − r and Duhem's theorem. Only a few universities teach full multireaction phase-rule counting; keep it brief.

figure.aria: A tree separating gas-phase, heterogeneous and simultaneous reaction equilibria, with the two example extents under the simultaneous branch.

chapters.example: Feed 1 mol pure A at 1 bar. Two independent ideal-gas reactions: A ⇌ B with K1 = 2.00; 2A ⇌ C with K2 = 0.500. Find equilibrium composition. Let extents ξ1 for first, ξ2 for second. n_A = 1−ξ1−2ξ2, n_B = ξ1, n_C = ξ2, nT = 1−ξ2. With P = P° = 1 bar, K1 = y_B/y_A = ξ1/(1−ξ1−2ξ2) = 2.00; K2 = y_C/y_A² = ξ2(1−ξ2)/(1−ξ1−2ξ2)² = 0.500. Solve: ξ1 = 0.603 mol, ξ2 = 0.0477 mol. Then n_A = 0.301 mol, n_B = 0.603 mol, n_C = 0.0477 mol; y_A = 0.317, y_B = 0.633, y_C = 0.0501.
chapters.trap: Giving pure solids a mole fraction in K, or using one extent for two reactions. Pure solid activity is 1; each independent reaction needs its own extent and K.
chapters.prereq: 7.3 K; 7.5 composition; Unit 5 fugacity and activity; Unit 6 phase equilibrium.
